RCS is defined as 4π times the ratio of scattered power density to incident power density in a specific direction.
Shaping techniques reduce RCS by deflecting radar waves away from the radar receiver through surface orientation.
Radar Absorbing Materials convert incident radar energy into heat, reducing reflected energy.
Active cancellation emits signals out of phase with radar echoes to destructively interfere and reduce RCS.
Microstrip antennas have high RCS due to their ground planes, which can be mitigated using metamaterials.
Frequency Selective Surfaces (FSS) can create bandstop or passband effects to control radar wave reflection.
Electromagnetic Bandgap (EBG) metamaterials prohibit electromagnetic wave propagation in certain frequency bands.
Negative Index Metamaterials exhibit negative permittivity and permeability, enabling unique wave manipulation.
Composite AMC surfaces with magnetodielectric substrates can achieve broadband RCS reduction with over 13 dB reduction and 93% bandwidth.
Wideband chessboard AMC structures can achieve -10 dB RCS reduction over 73% bandwidth.
Polarization conversion metamaterials can reduce in-band RCS by up to 16 dB compared to reference antennas.
Radar detection range decreases with the fourth root of RCS, so halving detection range requires reducing RCS by 16 times.
RAM coatings require uniform thickness and smoothness for effective RCS reduction and are often toxic.
Active cancellation techniques are more suitable for low-frequency RCSR due to broader scattering lobes.
Metamaterials enable antenna miniaturization, bandwidth expansion, gain enhancement, and RCS reduction simultaneously.
The proposed metamaterial unit cell includes a square loop and intersecting strips to reduce microstrip antenna RCS.
Modern radars operate across frequency bands from VHF (30-300 MHz) to Ka band (27-40 GHz), requiring broadband RCSR solutions.
Passive RCSR techniques are generally preferred for their simplicity and reliability over active methods.
The paper emphasizes combining shaping and RAM for effective stealth performance.
Metamaterials' electromagnetic responses differ from their constituent components due to engineered structure.
